title: The Metered Layer Under the Agent
description: Eight tools that price, route and fund the work agents do: GPU sessions, cheap CI, workflow deployment, gateways and open-source funding.
content:
# The Metered Layer Under the Agent

Agents have a cost structure that no one designed. A single afternoon of parallel sessions can open forty pull requests, run twelve test suites, and burn through a month of API credit before anyone notices.

The tools in this piece are the layer that meters it. None of them make an agent smarter. All of them change what happens when the agent does more than you planned.

## Compute by the hour

[[link:/tools/2235|Supercomputer]] sells GPU and CPU sessions that keep their files between runs. Stop a box when the work is done and billing stops while the files stay; resume when you need them. Rates are published per GPU-hour from a T4 up to a B200, and the site carries worked examples with reported results — nanoGPT to a 3.276 validation loss in 43 seconds, protein design at about 10.6 seconds per design, a robot policy fine-tune for roughly ten dollars.

## CI by the second

[[link:/tools/2236|Jog]] exists because GitHub-hosted runners bill by the minute and agents produce jobs that finish in twenty-five seconds. Change runs-on to jog and the site claims about 80 percent lower cost, with 5,000 free minutes a month, no subscription, per-second billing, and the action cache working without configuration. Private repositories only, which is exactly where agent-generated pull requests pile up.

## Funding by the boost

[[link:/tools/2237|boostmyagents]] solves a different cost problem: open-source maintainers whose AI plan runs out. Supporters buy a one-time boost through hosted Stripe Checkout from a badge in your README, and the capacity runs through bma-cli with Claude Code or Codex as a separate lane alongside your subscription. It pays in capacity rather than cash, which sidesteps a lot of accounting, and prompts are explicitly not inspected.

## Workflows by the run

[[link:/tools/2238|Whenever]] is where a repeated agent task becomes infrastructure. You describe the outcome, Claude Code, Codex or Cursor writes the workflow code, and it deploys through an MCP server. Deterministic steps and AI steps sit in the same flow, and you connect the accounts and decide when it goes live. Pricing is per run, which is honest about what a scheduled agent actually costs.

## Gateways by the request

[[link:/tools/2239|Portus]] consolidates three gateways into one data plane: Kubernetes routes, LLM providers and MCP tool servers behind a single install. It is written in Rust, passes all 130 Gateway API v1.6.2 conformance tests with no skips, and measured 224,173 requests per second at 2.98 ms p99 through three proxy pods on a 32-vCPU machine. The site also publishes where a competitor beats it on large plain-HTTP downloads, which is a good sign.

## Knowing what fits

[[link:/tools/2227|llmrun]] answers the question that precedes every local-model decision: which open models will actually run on this machine, and how good are they. It detects your hardware in the browser without uploading anything, then ranks open models by its own composite score with VRAM at Q4, tokens per second and the GPU each one needs. The score is llmrun's own metric, so treat it as a starting point rather than a verdict.

## The utilities an agent needs

[[link:/tools/2217|Castov]] is a developer toolkit that runs the same sixty-one utilities in the browser, the terminal and inside an agent. JSON to TypeScript, cron across timezones, JWT inspection, CIDR maths — all client-side with zero server logging, and an MCP server that exposes them to Cursor and Claude. The MCP surface is the interesting part: deterministic tools an agent can call without inventing an answer.

[[link:/tools/2228|Kitepod]] applies the same idea to a very specific stack. It connects the Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor plan you already pay for to every WordPress site you run, free and with no daily tool-call cap, across 51 tools covering pages, themes, page builders and WooCommerce. Changes are staged for preview and can be undone byte for byte.

## Why this layer matters

The pricing model tells you what a tool thinks it is. A subscription says the work is predictable. Per-second billing says the work is bursty. Per-completed-order, which is how a restaurant phone agent charges, says the outcome is what counts.

[[link:/tools/2236|Jog]] and [[link:/tools/2235|Supercomputer]] both price by the second because agent work is spiky. [[link:/tools/2238|Whenever]] prices by the run because a scheduled workflow either ran or did not. [[link:/tools/2237|boostmyagents]] prices in capacity because cash to an individual maintainer is a compliance problem.

That is a more useful signal than any benchmark. The metered layer is where the economics of agents become visible, and right now it is the layer moving fastest.
tldr: Supercomputer, Jog, boostmyagents, Whenever, Portus, llmrun, Castov and Kitepod all sit under the agent rather than inside it, charging by the second, the run or the GPU-hour.
